candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch on Elms | Texas Plant Disease Diagnostic Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch on elms is caused by the xylem-limited bacterium Xylella fastidiosa. It is identified by characteristic marginal leaf scorch, with symptoms progressing from older to younger leaves; affected leaves may curl and drop prematurely. The bacterium is spread by sharpshooters, leafhoppers, treehoppers, and spittlebugs.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch is caused by Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterium limited to the water-conducting xylem tissue. Affected leaves show browning along the margins with a band of yellow tissue between the scorched edge and healthy green tissue. As the disease progresses over years, branches die and the tree declines. Elm is among the commonly affected hosts.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch of Trees | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch of landscape trees is caused by Xylella fastidiosa and is spread by xylem-feeding insects such as leafhoppers, sharpshooters, and spittlebugs. Symptoms include marginal leaf scorch and premature leaf drop. There is no cure; management focuses on maintaining tree vigor, reducing stress, and removing severely affected trees.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch of Shade Trees | University of Illinois
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch (BLS) of shade trees, including elm, is caused by Xylella fastidiosa. The bacterium clogs the xylem so that not enough water reaches the leaves, producing marginal scorching. The pathogen is carried plant to plant by leafhoppers, sharpshooters, and spittlebugs.

candidate_sources.title: Black Spot of Elm â€“ Purdue Landscape Report
candidate_sources.snippet: Stegophora ulmea is a foliar disease of elms commonly known as black spot of elm, twig blight, and elm leaf scab. Characterized by chlorotic yellow spots 1 mm in diameter with a black center that develop early in spring; spots darken and become raised. Infects all Ulmus species and Japanese zelkova; most virulent on American elm (Ulmus americana). Management by sanitation, removing leaf debris, avoiding overhead watering, and pruning for air movement.

candidate_sources.title: Elm Black Spot - Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service
candidate_sources.snippet: Elm Black Spot is an important foliar disease in North American elms caused by the fungus formerly known as Gnomonia ulmea, now called Stegophora ulmea. Symptoms start as small whitish or yellowish flecks on the upper leaf surface that enlarge with black specks inside. Most elm species are susceptible; Ulmus americana is most susceptible. Management includes removing infected leaf debris and dead shoots, avoiding overhead irrigation, and preventive fungicides for nursery trees.

candidate_sources.title: Black Spot of Elm - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Black spot of elm caused by Stegophora ulmea. The fungus becomes active in the spring at temperatures of 45Â°F or above, releasing spores that infect newly unfolding leaves. Acervuli develop in the center of lesions and release white macroconidia maturing 10â€“20 days after infection. Overwinters in buds and discarded leaves. Can cause serious defoliation during wet, cool springs.

candidate_sources.title: Black Spot of Elm | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Black Spot of Elm caused by Stegophora ulmea (formerly Gnomonia ulmea). Foliar disease characterized by black raised spots on leaves, premature leaf drop, and twig infection. Cultural control through sanitation and removal of infected debris; chemical control with mancozeb, copper, or chlorothalonil for nursery trees.

candidate_sources.title: Stegophora ulmea (black spot of elm) - CABI Plantwise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Datasheet for Stegophora ulmea, the cause of black spot of elm (black leaf spot, elm anthracnose). Covers host range across Ulmus species and Zelkova, distribution, symptoms, biology, and management of this foliar pathogen of elm.

candidate_sources.title: Dutch elm disease | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Dutch elm disease is caused by two closely related fungi, Ophiostoma ulmi or O. novo-ulmi. The first symptom is wilting or 'flagging' of leaves, which curl, turn yellow then brown and drop. The fungus causes dark brown streaking in the sapwood. Spread tree to tree by elm bark beetles or via root grafts.

candidate_sources.title: Dutch Elm Disease (Ophiostoma ulmi [formerly Ceratocystis ulmi] and O. novo-ulmi) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Dutch Elm Disease caused by Ophiostoma ulmi [formerly Ceratocystis ulmi] and O. novo-ulmi. Detailed problem profile covering host plants, symptoms, and management of this destructive disease of elm.

candidate_sources.title: Dutch elm disease - APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Dutch elm disease educational lesson from the American Phytopathological Society. Covers the pathogens Ophiostoma ulmi and O. novo-ulmi, symptoms including flagging and vascular streaking, the elm bark beetle vectors, and disease management.

candidate_sources.title: Dutch Elm Disease | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Dutch elm disease is caused by Ophiostoma ulmi or O. novo-ulmi. Symptoms include wilting and flagging foliage, yellowing and browning leaves, and dark streaking in the sapwood. The fungus is spread by elm bark beetles and through root grafts. Management focuses on sanitation and removing beetle breeding sites.
